# Famous Quotes Search

In this lab, we’ll create an app that allows users to find famous quotes stored in a MySQL database by keyword, quote category, and author.  The quotes found will be displayed along with their corresponding author.  The screenshots below show the famous quotes found when searching for the keyword “life”

 

We’ll practice the following topics:

* Connecting to a MySQL database from an Express app  
* Retrieving data from a MySQL database  
* Populating form elements dynamically from a database  
* Creating a local web API to get and display data from a database  
* Displaying information in a modal

1. # Create Quotes Database

We’ll start by creating the database tables with the quotes and authors' data. You should already have access to a MySQL database on Heroku or another database server that allows remote access (refer to the [Creating a MySQL Database in Heroku](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10Esl3HNBaYnXrr3lSbJOgzRPPGgff4T8FRgyDkFy1cY/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.k9ioi31yr9hu)  tutorial).

If using Heroku, consider using [**phpMyAdmin**](https://csumb.space/phpMyAdmin/) to manage your database.  Optionally, you can use any other SQL client of your choice (e.g., [MySQL Workbench](https://www.mysql.com/products/workbench/), [Heidi](https://www.heidisql.com/))

When you create a free database in Heroku, its name will be a random combination of characters and numbers. In a real setting, you’d have the ability to give a more meaningful name to the database, such as “famous\_quotes”.  

If using phpMyAdmin, you must select your database by clicking it in the left-hand panel.  

Once the database is selected, click on the “SQL” tab to be able to run SQL statements.  
![][image1]  
[Copy and paste the SQL statements located in this file](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1h8uiv8GmNJi__Vy4G_9mlcLRN2HgFXX8Om9OZZa2WkQ/edit?usp=sharing) to create and populate the **q\_quotes** and **q\_authors** tables. 

The structure of each table is shown below.   
Both tables are related by the **authorId** column.  
Take a look at the records created to have an idea of their values.

| q\_authors | q\_quotes |
| ----- | :---: |

2. # Set up the App and Create the Folder Structure

     
1) In your IDE, create a new **Node** app. You can call it *quoteFinder* or any other name of your choice.

2) From the Terminal window, run the following command to generate the **package.json** file. 

    npm init \-y

3) Install the packages that the app will use. These are:

   **express**: to run the Express server   
   **ejs**:  to use the ejs templating engine for rendering web content  
   **mysql2**: to access and interact with a MySQL database  
   npm i express ejs mysql2  
   We’re using “i” as the shortcut for “install”

4) Create the folder structure of a default Express app.

   

   Within the app folder, create two more folders:    
   **public** and **views**

   Within the **public** folder, create three folders:  
   **css**, **img** and **js**

   Within the **views** folder, create the **partials** folder

5. #  Get Value Submitted by User

   

In this section, we’ll learn how to get the values submitted to an Express route through an HTML Form using the GET method.

There are several ways to submit data from the browser to an Express app. One way is using an **HTML Form,** such as the one we created:

    **\<form** action="**/searchByKeyword**"\>  
       Keyword:   
       \<input type="text" **name="**keyword**"**\>  
       \<button\>Search by Keyword\</button\>  
     \<**/form**\>

Observe that the form elements must be surrounded by the **\<form\>\</form\>** tag and the form element must include the **name** attribute.

There are two HTTP methods for submitting data through Forms: **GET** and **POST**.  
As the Method name implies, the GET method is used when the purpose of submitting the form is to get more data, whereas the POST method is used when the purpose is to store or update information. Also, the POST method should be used when sending confidential information or large amounts of data. 

In our case, since the purpose of submitting the form is to *get* all quotes containing a specified keyword, we are using the GET method.

By default, forms use the GET method, so we didn’t have to specify it in our Form. It’d have been the same typing :

     **\<form** **method="GET"** action="**/searchByKeyword**"\>

1) Add the **/searchByKeyword** route in the **index.mjs** file.  
   Run the app. When clicking on the button, you should see the “results coming soon…” message.  
   ![][image10]  
     
2) Modify the **/searchByKeyword** route to store the value submitted through the form in a variable. When using the GET method, all values are stored in the **req.query** object  (“req” is the abbreviation of request).  We use **req.query**.keyword because keyword corresponds to the value of the **name** attribute in the HTML Form.  
   ![][image11]

Run the app. Type anything in the text box, and when clicking on the button, you should see in the Express console the value typed (don’t use Nodemon so that you can see the output in the console)

6. #  Retrieve Quotes from DB by Keyword

Now, we need to write the SQL command to get all quotes containing the specified keyword. For this, we need to use the “LIKE” qualifier. Also, since we want to display the corresponding author below each quote, we need to join the two tables.

The SQL command should look like this:

[**SELECT**](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/select.html) quote, authorId, firstName, lastName  
**FROM** [q\_quotes](https://csumb.space/db/?server=u6354r3es4optspf.cbetxkdyhwsb.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com&username=mp26jo8kppunxiix&db=jkvs50o7ha454ro4&table=q_quotes)  
**NATURAL** [**JOIN**](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/join.html) [q\_authors](https://csumb.space/db/?server=u6354r3es4optspf.cbetxkdyhwsb.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com&username=mp26jo8kppunxiix&db=jkvs50o7ha454ro4&table=q_authors)  
**WHERE** quote [**LIKE**](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/string-comparison-functions.html#operator_like) '%**life**%'

Copy and paste the command above into your SQL client to verify that it works properly. You can replace “**life**” with any other keyword.  Recall that the “%” symbol represents a wildcard character and is part of the syntax of the LIKE qualifier.

1) Modify the **/searchByKeyword** route to include the SQL command to retrieve records based on the specified keyword:

   ![][image12]

2) Run the app. Try to look for keywords such as “life”, “world”, and “man”. You should see a few quotes.

3) Update the SQL command to prevent [SQL injection](https://www.acunetix.com/websitesecurity/sql-injection/). Recall that single quotes should be avoided as part of the SQL command to prevent anyone from injecting malicious queries. We’ll create a new array to store the actual value for *userKeyword*.

   ![][image13]

4) Run the app. The results should still be the same, but we are now preventing SQL injection.

8. # Search Quotes by Author

   In this section, we’ll implement the functionality to search all quotes by a specific author. We’ll display a dropdown menu with the authors’ first and last names, along with a new button. We’ll start by hard-coding a couple of authors’ names, then modify our dropdown menu to display the authors’ names from the database.  
     
1) Modify the **index.ejs** file to include a new form with a dropdown menu and a new button right below the “Search by Keyword” form  (lines 12 to 22\)

| ![][image17] |   \<form action\="/searchByAuthor"\>      \<select name="authorId"\>        \<option value="1"\>          Albert Einstein        \</option\>        \<option value="2"\>           Agatha Christie         \</option\>      \</select\>      \<button\>Search by Author\</button\>    \</form\>  |
| :---- | :---- |

   The value of the **action** attribute is **/searchByAuthor**, so we'll add the corresponding route next. 

   

   Observe that the \<select\> tag has the “**name**” attribute with the value of “**authorId**”.  In this way, when the form is submitted, the server will receive a parameter called “**authorId**,” which we can access via **req.query.authorId**

   Also, observe that the \<option\> tags include the “**value**”  attribute, and the value assigned to each author is the corresponding authorId (from the database). So, when selecting Albert Einstein, we’ll be assigning the value of “**1**” to “**authorId**” and then we’ll retrieve all quotes using that authorId.

2) Modify the **index.mjs** controller to add the new **/searchByAuthor** route. Let’s add it right below the **/searchByKeyword** route. Indeed, the code will be very similar. We just need to use “authorId” instead of “keyword”.

   ![][image18]

   Test the app, you should see the corresponding quotes for the author selected.

3) Let’s display the list of authors in the dropdown menu from the database instead of hard-coding them. We need to get their names before displaying the **index.ejs** view.  
   Modify the root route in the **index.mjs** file. We need to declare the function as asynchronous since we’ll be accessing the database. After getting the data from the database, we send it to the “**index.ejs**” view through the “**authors**” array (line 12\)

   ![][image19]

   

4) Modify the **index.ejs** view to loop through the “**authors**” array and to display the list of authors.  
   ![][image20]

   Observe that in lines 14 and 18 (for  loop), the EJS syntax does not include the equals sign  **\<%   %\>** instead of **\<%=   %\>**   

   The equals symbol is used only when displaying information, such as the value of a variable. No equals sign should be used for regular code, such as control structures (e.g., conditions and loops).  
     
   Run the app. You should see the list of authors in the dropdown menu and all the corresponding quotes for each of them.

9. # Create Local API to Display Author Info

In this section, we’ll implement a feature that lets users click an author's name to retrieve and display all their information from the database, using a local Web API to avoid refreshing the page.

1) Let’s start by making the authors’ names clickable. Open the **results.ejs** file and surround the first and last names with an anchor element  “\<a href\> \</a\>” 

   Observe that we are using a hashtag as the value of the “href” attribute to prevent the page from reloading when clicking the links.

   We’re also including the **id** attribute and assigning to it the corresponding authorId, so we can retrieve the quotes based on the authorId.

   

   Your output should look something like this:

   ![][image21]

   

   When viewing the Page Source in the browser,  you should see the corresponding authorId values within the “a” tag. It’s helpful to check the Page Source to ensure that the values are being assigned properly.

   

2) Next, we will add an event listener to every link. The event listener will retrieve the author information when the corresponding link is clicked.    
     
   2.1  Create a new **“scrips.js**” file within the “**public/js**” folder.

     For testing purposes, alert a message within the “script.js” file:  
     
        

     
   2.2 Embed the “**scripts.js**” file from the **results.ejs** file by adding the following line of code right before the closing \</body\> tag:

   ![][image22]

   2.3 Test whether the **script.js** file is accessed. Restart the app. You should see the alert message when searching for quotes. If no alert message pops up, check your syntax. Comment out or remove the alert message once you confirm that it’s working.

   2.4 Add  “click” event listeners by selecting all “a” elements and then looping through them. When any of the links is clicked, we’ll invoke the “**getAuthorInfo**” function. For testing purposes, let’s display the id of the author being clicked on by using “**alert(this.id)**”. The keyword “**this**” in this context refers to the link that is being clicked.  
   Test it, click on any author, and you should see the corresponding authorId.

   ![][image23]

3) Now, let’s work in the backend to implement the Web API that will retrieve all authors’ information based on the authorId. In the **index.mjs** file, add the following new route (code included below the screenshot)

   ![][image24]

   

| app.get('/api/author/:id', async (req, res) \=\> {   let authorId \= req.params.id;   let sql \= \`SELECT \*             FROM q\_authors             WHERE authorId \= ?\`;              let \[rows\] \= await conn.query(sql, \[authorId\]);   res.send(rows) }); |
| :---- |

   

   Observe that the route is using a “route parameter”, which consists of a colon and the name of the parameter (:id). To access its value, we use “req.**params**” and then the name of the parameter (.id)

   Also, observe that we’re not rendering the data in a view, but we’re using “send” to send the raw data in JSON format.

   Test the api by running the app and then adding **/api/author/1** to the url. You should see all the information for the first author in JSON format. Test a few other values in the url.

4) Come back to the “**script.js**” file. Update the “**getAuthorInfo()**” function to use the local API we just added. Make sure to declare the function as “**async**”

   ![][image25]  
     
   Open the “Inspect Tool.” When you click any author link, you should be able to see their information in the console.

   ![][image26]

5) Display the author's info on the web page. Instead of displaying the info in the console, we’ll display it on the actual page.

   5.1 Add an HTML element as a placeholder in the **results.ejs** file

   ![][image27]

   5.2  Add/append the author information in the HTML element placeholder.  Modify the “**getAuthorInfo()**” function located in **script.js** file:

   ![][image28]

   Test it. The author's information should be displayed at the bottom of the **results.ejs** file when clicking on any of the authors. Display all remaining fields in the “**getAuthorInfo()**” function (dob, dod, bio, etc).

10. # Use a Modal to Display the Author Data.

    In this section, we’ll use a modal window to display the author information on top of the content of the page. For this, we’ll use Bootstrap since it provides all of the code we need.  
      
    1\) Embed the Bootstrap CSS and JS files. 

        Go to [https://getbootstrap.com/](https://getbootstrap.com/), scroll down to the “Include via CDN” section and copy the CSS and JS links by clicking on their corresponding clipboard icons.

    Paste them within the “**header.ejs**” partial.  
    

      
2\) Access the “**Modal**” component. In the Bootstrap website, click on “**Doc**” from the top navigation menu and then click on “**Components**” from the menu on the left.

Scroll down the list of components and then click on “**Modal**”. Scroll down the “**Modal Live Demo**”

3\) Copy the code of the Modal Live Demo example, which should look something like this:

![][image29]

4\) Paste the Modal code in the “**results.ejs**” file and make the following changes (see these changes in red on the following page)

* Add an **id** with the value of “**authorModal**” to the div container.  
* Change the “**modal-title**” content to read “Author Information”  
* Move the “**authorInfo**” div container we created before and put it inside “**modal-body**”


\<\!-- Modal \--\>  
\<div class="modal fade"  **id="authorModal"** tabindex="-1" aria-labelledby="exampleModalLabel" aria-hidden="true"\>  
  \<div class="modal-dialog"\>  
    \<div class="modal-content"\>  
      \<div class="modal-header"\>  
        \<h1 class="modal-title fs-5" id="exampleModalLabel"\>**Author Information**\</h1\>  
        \<button type="button" class="btn-close" data-bs-dismiss="modal" aria-label="Close"\>\</button\>  
      \</div\>  
      \<div class="modal-body"\>  
         **\<div id=”authorInfo”\>\</div\>**  
      \</div\>  
      \<div class="modal-footer"\>  
        \<button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary" data-bs-dismiss="modal"\>Close\</button\>  
        \<button type="button" class="btn btn-primary"\>Save changes\</button\>  
      \</div\>  
    \</div\>  
  \</div\>  
\</div\>  
            
5\) Launch the modal using JavaScript. If you scroll down the “Modal” page in Bootstrap, you’ll notice that there is a section titled “Via JavaScript” which includes the code to launch the modal using JS. Add the following two lines of code at the beginning of the “**getAuthorInfo**” function, in the **scripts.js** file  (code below the screenshot)  
![][image30]  
var myModal \= new bootstrap.Modal(document.getElementById(**'authorModal'**));  
 myModal.show();

These two lines of code will launch the modal and display the information of the selected author.  You can now remove the button to trigger the modal since it’s not needed.
